questions.prompt: What is the capital city of North Korea?

hints.nudge: A capital city is where a country’s government meets. The other three are capital cities too, of other countries.
hints.whereToLook: Look in the opening paragraphs of the North Korea article.

questions.proof: The capital city of North Korea is Pyongyang, which is also the largest city in the country.

questions.prompt: Which of these countries shares a border with North Korea?

hints.nudge: Two countries are neighbours when you can walk from one into the other. Picture North Korea on the globe and look at what it touches.
hints.whereToLook: Look in the “The Korean War” part of the North Korea article.

questions.proof: With the help of the other countries, South Korea took back their land, and even much of North Korea, up to the Yalu River, which forms the border between North Korea and China.

questions.prompt: Which language is an official language of North Korea?

hints.nudge: An official language is the one used in schools, courts and government. The other three are spoken in other countries.
hints.whereToLook: Look in the “Culture and Religion” part of the North Korea article.

questions.proof: During the Japanese rule, Koreans were forced to learn and speak Japanese, adopt the Japanese family name system and Shinto religion, and were forbidden to write or speak the Korean language in schools, businesses, or public places.

questions.prompt: Fill the gap: “North Korea had ties with China and _____ but never was formally allied with either and became more isolated over time.”

hints.nudge: In the sentence the missing word sits beside “China”. It names one thing, not an action.
hints.whereToLook: Look in the opening paragraphs of the North Korea article.

questions.proof: North Korea had ties with China and Russia but never was formally allied with either and became more isolated over time.

questions.prompt: Fill the gap: “Very recently, North Korea's food aid stopped after the government launched a satellite in April _____.”

hints.nudge: It is a year in the twenty-first century.
hints.whereToLook: Look in the “Politics and Government” part of the North Korea article.

questions.proof: Very recently, North Korea's food aid stopped after the government launched a satellite in April 2012.
